title: Find Substring with Given Hash Value
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing the full polynomial per window versus rolling the hash right to left without division.

sections.title: Find Substring with Given Hash Value

content.title: Find Substring with Given Hash Value

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a string s of lowercase letters, and parameters power, modulo, k, and a target hashValue, find the substring of s with length k whose hash, computed using the formula val(s[0]) plus val(s[1]) times power, plus val(s[2]) times power squared, and so on up through position k minus 1, all taken modulo the given modulo, equals hashValue.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a string s of lowercase letters, and parameters power, modulo, k, and a target hashValue, find the substring of s with length k whose hash, computed using the formula val(s[0]) plus val(s[1]) times power, plus val(s[2]) times power squared, and so on up through position k minus 1, all taken modulo the given modulo, equals hashValue.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the One Combination That Unlocks a Specific Code
blocks.text: Like testing a sliding window of dial positions against a specific target combination, where each dial contributes to an overall code value in a weighted, positional way, searching for the one window whose combined code matches exactly.

blocks.text: Edge case: k equal to the length of s
With only one possible window covering the entire string, that single window must be the answer, since there is no other window to compare it against.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask which direction a rolling hash can safely move in in modular arithmetic, and why that direction matters here specifically.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Distinct Echo Substrings and Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String already showed that a hash can roll from one window to the next in O(1), rather than being rebuilt from scratch.

Observation 2: Rolling this specific hash forward, left to right, would require dividing out the old leading term by power, and division under an arbitrary modulus generally needs a modular inverse, which does not always exist.

Observation 3: Scanning from the end of the string backward avoids this entirely, removing the term that is about to leave the window on the right only ever needs a subtraction and a multiplication by a precomputed power, and adding the new character joining on the left as the new lowest order term only ever needs a multiplication by power and an addition, no division anywhere.

Observation 4: Tracing s equal to "fbxzaad" backward reveals something important, the window "bxz" at index 1 happens to share the exact same hash value, 32, as the true answer "fbx" at index 0, so the scan must continue all the way through to index 0, continuing to overwrite the recorded answer on every match, rather than stopping at the first one found, to correctly end on the leftmost match, "fbx".

Recognizing that rolling the hash backward avoids ever needing a modular inverse, and that the scan must continue to the very end overwriting its answer on every match to guarantee the leftmost one wins, is what makes this approach both efficient and correct.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every possible window of length k, compute its hash completely from scratch using the full polynomial formula, and compare it directly against the target hash value.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every starting position where a window of length k fits, compute that window's hash using the full formula from position 0 of the window through position k minus 1.
Compare the computed hash against hashValue.
Return the first window whose hash matches.

codes.python:
def sub_str_hash(s, power, modulo, k, hash_value):
    n = len(s)
    for start in range(n - k + 1):
        h = 0
        p = 1
        for i in range(k):                                          # recompute the full polynomial from scratch
            val = ord(s[start + i]) - ord('a') + 1
            h = (h + val * p) % modulo
            p = (p * power) % modulo
        if h == hash_value:
            return s[start:start + k]
    return ""


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "fbxzaad"
    power = 31
    modulo = 100
    k = 3
    hash_value = 32
    print(sub_str_hash(s, power, modulo, k, hash_value))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Windows are scanned left to right, so returning immediately on the first match found already guarantees the leftmost matching window is returned.
Each window's hash is built up term by term using a running power of the base, directly matching the formula's definition.
A fresh hash and a fresh running power are used for every window, so no information from a previous window is reused at all.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every window's hash is computed exactly as the formula defines it, so the leftmost matching window is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), recomputing the full k term polynomial for each of roughly n windows.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the answer substring.
Limitation: consecutive windows overlap in all but one character, yet the hash is fully recomputed from the formula's very first term every single time, instead of being updated incrementally.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: recomputing the entire k term polynomial for every window ignores that consecutive windows share all but one character.

Why rolling forward, left to right, is awkward: removing the old leading term requires dividing by power under the modulus, which needs a modular inverse that may not exist for an arbitrary modulo.

What rolling backward fixes: removing the term about to leave the window becomes a subtraction and a multiplication by a precomputed power, since that term is now the highest order one, and adding a new lowest order term only ever needs a multiply and an add.

The core idea: scan from the end of the string toward the beginning, rolling the hash with only multiplication, addition, and subtraction, and keep overwriting the recorded answer on every match so the scan naturally finishes on the leftmost one.

Rolling the hash forward normally requires dividing by power to remove the old leading term, which is unsafe under modular arithmetic without computing a modular inverse. This is avoided entirely by scanning from the end of the string backward instead: rolling the hash to the left only ever requires multiplying the current hash by power and adding the new character's value, both of which are safe operations under a simple modulo, with no division needed at all.
9. Optimized Solution
Scan from the end of the string, rolling the hash left one character at a time using only multiplication and addition.
Dry run for s = "fbxzaad", power = 31, modulo = 100, k = 3, hashValue = 32

blocks.caption: Optimized: roll the hash from right to left using only multiplication and addition, no division

codes.python:
def sub_str_hash(s, power, modulo, k, hash_value):
    n = len(s)

    def val(ch):
        return ord(ch) - ord('a') + 1

    current_hash = 0
    high_power = pow(power, k - 1, modulo)
    for i in range(n - 1, n - k - 1, -1):
        current_hash = (current_hash * power + val(s[i])) % modulo    # build the very last window directly

    result_start = n - k if current_hash == hash_value else -1
    for start in range(n - k - 1, -1, -1):
        current_hash = (current_hash - val(s[start + k]) * high_power % modulo) % modulo
        current_hash = (current_hash * power + val(s[start])) % modulo   # roll left with only multiply and add
        current_hash %= modulo
        if current_hash == hash_value:
            result_start = start                                          # keep overwriting, never stop early
    return s[result_start:result_start + k]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = "fbxzaad"
    power = 31
    modulo = 100
    k = 3
    hash_value = 32
    print(sub_str_hash(s, power, modulo, k, hash_value))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because removing the term about to leave the window on the right, now sitting at the highest power position, only ever needs subtracting that term's exact contribution (its value times the precomputed highest power) before multiplying the remaining hash by power and adding the new character joining on the left, reproducing the exact same value the full formula would give for that window, with no division ever required; and because the scan continues all the way to index 0 without stopping early, whichever match has the smallest starting index is guaranteed to be the very last one recorded.

Time: O(n), a single backward pass with constant work per step.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the answer substring.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Handles Multiple Matches","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (recompute per window)","O(n times k)","O(1)","Yes, returns the first (leftmost) match naturally, scanning forward","Correct, but slow for large n or k."],["Optimized (right to left rolling hash)","O(n)","O(1)","Yes, by never stopping early while scanning backward","The expected answer, avoiding any modular inverse."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The key trick is direction: rolling a hash window forward normally needs a modular inverse to undo the highest order term, which is awkward and slow, while rolling backward only ever needs a multiply and an add, since the new term being added always becomes the new lowest order term instead.
Common Mistakes

items: Attempting to roll the hash left to right the naive way, which requires dividing by power under a modulus, a genuinely harder operation requiring a modular inverse that does not always exist for an arbitrary modulo.
Forgetting to take a proper positive modulo after a subtraction, since intermediate values can go negative and produce incorrect comparisons.
Stopping at the first match found while scanning backward instead of continuing all the way to index 0, which can return the wrong window when more than one window shares the same hash value.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explain clearly why scanning backward avoids the need for a modular inverse, since recognizing this specific direction trick is the entire point of this problem beyond a standard rolling hash.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you roll this hash without a modular inverse", think: scan right to left, where removing the outgoing term is a subtraction, not a division.
If the interviewer says "what if more than one window matches", think: keep scanning to the very end and keep overwriting the recorded answer, so the leftmost match naturally survives.
If the interviewer says "why does this specific direction avoid needing an inverse", think: the term leaving the window from the right is always the current highest power term, removable by a plain subtraction, while the new term joining on the left is always the new lowest power term, addable directly.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does rolling the hash from right to left avoid the need for a modular inverse, while rolling left to right would require one?
Why must the scan continue all the way to index 0 instead of stopping at the first match found?
How would this approach change if modulo were guaranteed to be prime?
How would you adapt this technique to search for the rightmost matching window instead of the leftmost?
How would you extend this approach to find every window matching the target hash value, not just the leftmost one?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Distinct Echo Substrings and Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String, whose rolling hash techniques are extended here with the added twist of rolling in the direction that avoids a modular inverse.

Any problem involving a rolling computation under a modulus, where checking whether the update needs a division (and therefore a modular inverse) versus only multiplication and addition determines which direction is safe to roll in.

Any "find the leftmost match among possibly several" problem, where continuing a scan to completion and always overwriting on a match, rather than stopping early, is the standard way to guarantee the correct one is kept.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n times k) time, O(1) extra space. Optimized (right to left rolling hash): O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a rolling hash computed right to left, avoiding any need for a modular inverse, keeping the leftmost matching window.

Core Idea: rolling the hash backward only ever needs multiplication, addition, and subtraction, never division, and continuing the scan to completion while always overwriting on a match guarantees the leftmost match is the one kept.
Time: O(n times k) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra for both approaches.

Most Important Observation: the direction a rolling computation moves in can determine whether an update needs a division (and a modular inverse) or only multiplication and addition, and choosing the safe direction is the whole trick.

Interview Difficulty: the rolling hash mechanics themselves are standard; recognizing why the backward direction is specifically required here, and why the scan must never stop early, is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: roll right to left with multiply and add only, and never stop scanning early, since the leftmost match must win.
